{{Short description|Statistical measure to determine how suited data is for factor analysis}}
The '''Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) test''' is a statistical measure to determine how suited data is for [[factor analysis]]. The test measures sampling adequacy for each variable in the model and the complete model. The statistic is a measure of the proportion of variance among variables that might be common variance. The higher the proportion, the higher the KMO-value, the more suited the data is to factor analysis.<ref name="ibm">{{cite web |url=https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/spss-statistics/28.0.0?topic=detection-kmo-bartletts-test |access-date=15 February 2022|title=KMO and Bartlett's Test|website=[[IBM]] }}</ref>

== History ==


[[Henry Felix Kaiser|Henry Kaiser]] introduced a Measure of Sampling Adequacy (MSA) of factor analytic data matrices in 1970.<ref name="start">{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/BF02291817 |title=A second generation little jiffy|year=1970|last1=Kaiser|first1=Henry F.|journal=Psychometrika|volume=35|issue=4|pages=401–415|s2cid=121850294 }}</ref> Kaiser and Rice then modified it in 1974.<ref name="k2">{{cite journal |doi=10.1177/001316447403400115 |title=Little Jiffy, Mark Iv|year=1974|last1=Kaiser|first1=Henry F.|last2=Rice|first2=John|journal=Educational and Psychological Measurement|volume=34|pages=111–117|s2cid=144844099 }}</ref>
==Measure of sampling adequacy==


The measure of sampling adequacy is calculated for each indicator as


:<math>MSA_j = \frac{\displaystyle \sum_{k\neq j} r_{jk}^2}{\displaystyle \sum_{k\neq j} r_{jk}^2+\sum_{k\neq j} p_{jk}^2}</math> 

and indicates to what extent an indicator is suitable for a factor analysis.

==Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin criterion==

: The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin criterion is calculated and returns values between 0 and 1. 
:
:<math>KMO = \frac{\displaystyle \underset{j\neq k}{\sum\sum} r_{jk}^2}{\displaystyle \underset{j\neq k}{\sum\sum} r_{jk}^2+\underset{j\neq k}{\sum\sum} p_{jk}^2}</math> 

Here <math>r_{jk}</math> is the correlation between the variable in question and another, and <math>p_{jk}</math> is the [[partial correlation]].

This is a function of the squared elements of the `image' matrix compared to the squares of the original correlations. The overall MSA as well as estimates for each item are found. The index is known as the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) index.<ref name="Factor">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9781315799476 |title=Factor Analysis|year=2013|last1=Cureton|first1=Edward E.|last2=d'Agostino|first2=Ralph B.|isbn=9781315799476}}</ref>

== Interpretation of result ==
In flamboyant fashion, Kaiser proposed that a KMO&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.9 was marvelous, in the 0.80s, meritorious, in the 0.70s, middling, in the 0.60s, mediocre, in the 0.50s, miserable, and less than 0.5 would be unacceptable. <ref name="k2"/> In general, KMO values between 0.8 and 1 indicate the sampling is adequate. KMO values less than 0.6 indicate the sampling is not adequate and that remedial action should be taken. In contrast, others set this cutoff value at 0.5.<ref name="review1974">{{cite journal |doi=10.1037/h0036316 |title=When is a correlation matrix appropriate for factor analysis? Some decision rules|year=1974|last1=Dziuban|first1=Charles D.|last2=Shirkey|first2=Edwin C.|journal=Psychological Bulletin|volume=81|issue=6|pages=358–361}}</ref> A KMO value close to zero means that there are large partial correlations compared to the sum of correlations. In other words, there are widespread correlations which would be a large problem for factor analysis.<ref name="ibm" />

An alternative measure of whether a matrix is factorable is the [[Bartlett test]], which tests the degree that the matrix deviates from an [[identity matrix]].<ref name="ibm"/>

== Example in R ==
If the following is run in [[R (programming language)|R]] with the library(psych)

<syntaxhighlight lang="R">
library(psych)
set.seed(5L)
five.samples <- data.frame("A"=rnorm(100), "B"=rnorm(100), "C"=rnorm(100),
                           "D"=rnorm(100), "E"=rnorm(100))
cor(five.samples)
KMO(five.samples)
</syntaxhighlight>

The following is produced:

<syntaxhighlight lang="R">
Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin factor adequacy
Call: KMO(r = five.samples)
Overall MSA =  0.53
MSA for each item = 
   A    B    C    D    E 
0.52 0.56 0.52 0.48 0.54 
</syntaxhighlight>

This shows that the data is not that suited to Factor Analysis.<ref name="R">{{cite web |url=https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/psych/versions/2.1.3/topics/KMO |access-date=14 May 2021|title=KMO function - RDocumentation}}</ref>
